claim: declarations that: Proceedings in the Market Misconduct Tribunal are criminal in nature for the purposes of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance; the requirements of Article 10 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance in respect of a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal are not satisfied by the Market Misconduct Tribunal; the abrogation of the privilege against self-incrimination of a person the subject of investigation is disproportionate; and it is lawful for a person the subject of an investigation to refuse to answer any question on the grounds that such answer may incriminate him
requested_remedy: declarations that: Proceedings in the Market Misconduct Tribunal are criminal in nature for the purposes of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance; the requirements of Article 10 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance in respect of a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal are not satisfied by the Market Misconduct Tribunal; the abrogation of the privilege against self-incrimination of a person the subject of investigation is disproportionate; and it is lawful for a person the subject of an investigation to refuse to answer any question on the grounds that such answer may incriminate him

facts.F1: Mr. Koon received a notice requiring him to attend an interview by an Investigator of the Securities and Futures Commission on 28 December 2006.
facts.F2: The notice informed Mr. Koon that he was a person under investigation in respect of offences of false trading and stock price rigging and/or stock market manipulation.
facts.F3: The notice required Mr. Koon to attend at a specific time on a specific date and to answer questions relating to the matters under investigation.
facts.F4: Mr. Koon was granted leave to bring judicial review proceedings in respect of the issue of notice and the requirement to answer questions.
facts.F5: Counsel for Mr. Koon contended that the notice is in breach of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance in two respects: under Article 11(2)(g) and under Article 10.
facts.F6: The relevant provision of the Securities and Futures Ordinance requiring Mr. Koon to answer the questions put to him by the SFC investigators is s 183.
facts.F7: The provision requires, inter alia, that the person under investigation must attend before the investigator at the time and place the investigator requires and answer any question relating to the matters under investigation that the investigator may raise with him.
facts.F8: It is an offence, without reasonable excuse, to fail to attend before the investigator as required and to answer questions under s 184.
facts.F9: The investigation being undertaken by the SFC may result in five different scenarios: the investigation may conclude and no criminal charges be brought against any person nor may any person or matter be brought before the Market Misconduct Tribunal; criminal proceedings may be brought against Mr. Koon; criminal proceedings may be brought against persons other than Mr. Koon; Market Misconduct Tribunal proceedings may be brought against Mr. Koon; or Market Misconduct Tribunal proceedings may be brought against persons other than Mr. Koon.
facts.F10: The court held that issues as to the abrogation of the right to silence or the impartiality of the Market Misconduct Tribunal have not yet arisen.
facts.F11: The testimonial immunity contained in the Bill of Rights is preserved in the event of a criminal prosecution under the Ordinance.
facts.F12: Section 187(2) of the Ordinance renders Mr. Koon's compelled answers inadmissible in those criminal proceedings.
facts.F13: No issue has arisen for consideration until such time as proceedings are commenced in the Market Misconduct Tribunal.

reference_issues: Whether the notice requiring Mr. Koon to attend an interview and answer questions is in breach of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance
Whether the Market Misconduct Tribunal proceedings constitute criminal proceedings
Whether the abrogation of the privilege against self-incrimination of a person the subject of investigation is disproportionate
Whether the requirements of Article 10 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance in respect of a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal are satisfied by the Market Misconduct Tribunal

facts.F3: According to PW2, 3 to 5 males ran towards him, and his attention was focused on the 1st Appellant, who was holding a long object (later known to be a golf club).
facts.F4: PW2 said he saw the 1st Appellant throw the golf club away and continue to run towards his direction.
facts.F5: An important point in cross-examination of PW2 was that he had said there were 'arrest forms' in Sham Shui Po Police Station, which was used by PW1 when he arrested the 1st Defendant, but he did not use it.

facts.F7: PW3 claimed that he saw the 2nd Appellant holding a beef knife and that the 2nd Appellant had thrown away the beef knife and PW3 gave chase without losing sight of the 2nd Appellant, and finally arrested the 2nd Appellant at a set of traffic lights.

facts.F1: The defendant was convicted of dealing with property known or believed to represent the proceeds of an indictable offence, contrary to section 5(1) and 25(1) and (3) of the Organised and Serious Crimes Ordinance.
facts.F2: The amount involved was $3,037,249.90, which is the Hong Kong dollar equivalent of a sum of US$380,406.09 that was remitted into the account of the defendant's company, Sun Polo Investment Consultant Limited, on 19 June 2008.
facts.F3: The sum of US$380,406.09 represents the proceeds of a theft in the United States of America, where a Mr and Mrs Scott had obtained a home equity line of credit of US$400,000 from their bank, the Severn Savings Bank, situated in Baltimore, Maryland.
facts.F4: On 16 June 2008, Severn Savings Bank received an application purportedly signed by Mr Scott requesting that a loan of US$380,438.13 from the line of credit be deposited into Sun Polo’s US dollar account in Hong Kong.
facts.F5: Neither Mr nor Mrs Scott had applied for this loan nor had they authorised anyone to do so.
facts.F6: On the day the sum of money arrived in Hong Kong, the defendant went to the Standard Chartered Bank and converted the US dollars into HK$3,037,249.90, the amount referred to in the charge.
facts.F7: The defendant then went from one branch of Standard Chartered Bank to another in Kowloon and drew out almost the whole of this sum of Hong Kong dollars in cash.
facts.F8: During the police interview, the defendant claimed that he believed the money was being used to finance the purchase of a Chinese painting by an American named Mark Grande from a mainlander, a Mr Gu Junyang.
facts.F9: The defendant admitted that he received a reward of about US$20,000 simply for allowing Sun Polo’s bank account to be used to finance the transaction.
facts.F10: The defendant knew that the account provided during the police interview was untrue.
facts.F11: The original offence was committed in the United States and the proceeds remitted out of the United States to Hong Kong.
facts.F12: The offence was a carefully planned and sophisticated crime, with the defendant involved in the fabrication of documents designed to deceive investigators.
facts.F13: The defendant has a long criminal record, which includes offences of fraud.
facts.F14: The defendant was recently sentenced to 5 years’ imprisonment for an offence of causing a copy of a false instrument.

reference_issues: Whether the defendant knew that he was dealing with the proceeds of a criminal activity.
Whether the defendant's involvement in the offence was a serious aggravating feature.
